d0662ea4-7a05-474b-97b6-e5992abd40bf.recap: Macro investor Ed Dowd argues private credit has effectively become the new junk-bond market, but opaque, illiquid and self-marked -- riskier credits have migrated there from public high yield, leaving public HY spreads artificially tight while masking deterioration. He cites widening CCC spreads (noted by Gundlach, who called it 'garbage lending'), loans marked at par one month and near-zero the next, and rising fund redemptions with stalling inflows as evidence a credit-loss cycle (per a PIMCO note) is beginning. He traces the root to weak 'K-shaped' consumer fundamentals (First Brands, Tricolor bankruptcies), unreliable labor data (QCEW revisions showing non-farm payrolls off by 8 and 4 standard deviations in 2024-25), and private credit's 50-75% two-year asset growth funded by bank lending, which JPMorgan is reportedly now curtailing. He flags contagion channels: CLO downgrades forcing institutional sales, banks pulling credit lines, and rising demand for significant risk transfers (SRTs) as insiders quietly hedge while publicly downplaying risk -- a pattern he likens to pre-2008 CDS demand. He connects this to AI: the last credit impulse funded data-center/chip capex (Morgan Stanley estimated $1.5tn in external financing needed), semiconductors are now 19% of the S&P 500, and AI/AI-adjacent names are 40-45% of market cap, leaving equities vulnerable to a credit-driven drawdown. He also flags falling 3-month T-bill rates and a strengthening dollar (dollar shortage) as things to watch, expecting Fed cuts within six months.
terms: SRT -- significant risk transfer, a structure banks use to transfer credit risk on a loan portfolio off their balance sheet
CLO -- collateralized loan obligation, a securitization backed by a pool of leveraged loans
QCEW -- Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, a lagging but comprehensive benchmark dataset used to revise non-farm payroll estimates
CCC -- a below-investment-grade credit rating tier indicating high default risk

d1060f69-9463-4c54-b6ee-96adb50949a6.recap: Economic forecaster Harry Dent argues markets are in the "everything bubble," the largest in history, driven by 45- and 90-year technology/demographic cycles and generational spending peaks (workers spend most from age 20-46). He says the 2008 downturn was the start of a 13-14 year demographic-driven depression that governments masked with roughly $31 trillion in stimulus and money printing since 2008, artificially extending the bubble into real estate, stocks, and even gold/silver. Dent predicts a crash later in the 2020s -- potentially visible by October, before US midterms -- that could take the S&P 500 down as much as 90% and real estate down 60-80%, worse than 1929-32, because this bubble is broader and more debt-fueled. He dismisses gold as a safe haven, noting it fell 30-40% in the second half of 2008 and has itself become bubbly (up from $1600 to $5600), instead favoring long-dated US Treasuries (TLT, or 30-year bonds) as the only asset that rose materially in the 2008 crisis, alongside T-bills for safety and yield. Post-crash, he favors India and Southeast Asia over China (which he says has 22% empty real estate and an overleveraged population) as the next demographic growth story, and would rebuy US tech (QQQ) at depressed valuations. Tactically he suggests SQQQ (triple-short Nasdaq) to catch the first crash wave, then rotating into TLT.

d1acf7da-685f-4835-a0fd-1dc3718e6696.recap: The host argues the real energy story isn't crude oil prices but the crack spread -- the margin between crude and refined products like diesel, which has hit record highs even as crude looks tame. Refineries, not crude supply, are the bottleneck: US refiners ran at 98% capacity (highest in nearly 8 years) in late August, unable to safely push higher, while global refined product losses are estimated at 2-4.7 million barrels per day (IEA) due to Hormuz disruptions, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, Moscow's export suspension, and China protecting domestic supply. US distillate inventories are at their lowest for this time of year since 1980s EIA records began, even as the US exports aggressively to meet global demand. The diesel 3-2-1 crack spread has exceeded $100/barrel, historically extreme. Simultaneously, US gasoline demand fell for a second consecutive summer (8.9 mb/d in August vs 9.05 and 9.12 in prior two years), which the host links to weakening labor data -- JOLTS hiring rate below 5.1 million, quits falling to ~3.06 million, hiring ratio at 1.84% of working-age population, all consistent with a stagnant 'no-hire economy.' The thesis: rather than generating broad inflation, the energy shock is colliding with a strained consumer, producing demand destruction -- retailers (Walmart, Kroger, Aldi) cutting prices and promotions rather than passing on costs. With peak diesel season (harvest, heating) approaching amid record-low inventories, the host expects elevated, volatile diesel cracks but disinflationary pressure elsewhere in the economy.
terms: Crack spread -- the estimated gross margin from refining crude oil into products, commonly measured via the 3-2-1 ratio (3 barrels crude to 2 gasoline + 1 distillate)
JOLTS -- the US Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, a BLS report on hires, quits, and openings
IEA -- the International Energy Agency

dcaf7a31-ce64-4beb-9873-be1f13c7278a.recap: This is an author interview with William Cohen about his book "Money to Burn," on Leon Black, Apollo, and Mark Rowan. Most of the conversation is biographical and narrative: Cohen's method of getting powerful subjects to talk on the record, the personal histories of Leon Black (son of Eli Black, an Orthodox rabbi turned United Brands CEO who died by suicide amid the United Brands/Chiquita bribery scandal) and Mark Rowan, Apollo's founding out of Drexel Burnham after Michael Milken's junk-bond empire collapsed, and Leon Black's contested succession planning, including his gifting of 58 million Apollo shares to Rowan and Josh Harris to engineer a credible succession story. A substantial segment covers Leon Black's $158 million in payments to Jeffrey Epstein, ostensibly for tax and estate advice, and Cohen's effort to adjudicate whether that explanation is credible. The most market-relevant portion describes how Rowan and Jim Belardi built Athene, an annuity insurer, explicitly to solve the classic bank problem of borrowing short and lending long by matching annuity liability duration to invested assets, then merged it into Apollo to fund a private credit engine. Cohen notes Apollo's assets have shifted from mostly private equity to roughly $850 billion of private credit versus $150 billion of private equity, spanning deals like the Nvidia-linked $500 billion lending facility and Yankees debt refinancing. Cohen closes by flagging that if annuitants ever demanded withdrawals en masse despite penalties, Apollo could face a run-on-the-bank-style dynamic, drawing parallels to 2008 and Silicon Valley Bank.
terms: CLO -- collateralized loan obligation, a securitization backed by a pool of leveraged loans

e15e7ba0-774d-42b6-adeb-f5cbec92754a.recap: Mike Pyle, deputy head of BlackRock's portfolio management group and a former US deputy national security advisor, discusses how the macro regime has shifted since his earlier BlackRock stint (2014-2021). He frames today's environment as "supply driven" -- shaped by pandemic-era supply-chain shocks, the Russia-Ukraine war, the Iran-linked energy shock, and the AI capex boom -- in contrast to the demand-deficient 2010s, when central banks suppressed rates and volatility, growth risk dominated inflation risk, and bonds provided strong equity diversification. He argues fiscal policy has become more activist post-2010s, as policymakers overcorrected for perceived under-stimulus after the GFC. On AI, he sees current bottleneck-driven earnings among suppliers to hyperscalers as likely to compress over time as competition and new supply relax constraints, though he expects a durable earnings path given AI demand still outstripping supply; he doesn't see current forward valuations as stretched (citing sub-10x forward multiples for some memory firms). On rates, he flags an active debate about whether AI-driven productivity gains will be disinflationary (1990s-style) while also possibly pushing the neutral real rate higher, versus a minority view of downward pressure on real rates -- with the answer still unclear via real-time productivity data. On portfolio construction, he argues bonds' role has shifted from duration-based diversification to income generation, with diversification instead sought via market-neutral/multi-strategy hedge funds, and describes growing client interest in portable alpha and total portfolio approaches (TPA) that blend public/private income and alpha overlays atop equity beta.

key_claims: Nelson: JPMorgan Chase's reserve balances at the Fed fell from $400bn (end-2023) to $100bn (end-2025), partly because repo rates rose relative to IORB, making it financially sensible to shrink reserves.

Nelson: Fed staff told the FOMC pre-2019 that structural reserve demand was ~$1 trillion; it is now roughly $3 trillion, and he believes it could return toward $1tn (or somewhat higher given economic growth) with the right liquidity-regulation changes.
Nelson: the 2019 repo-market volatility and 2023 QT slowdown were both predictable 'potholes' from coupon-settlement reserve drains that the Fed failed to pre-empt with timely open market operations.

Nelson: as of a 2024 Fed FAQ, banks can now count standing repo operations, the discount window, and FHLB advances toward satisfying internal liquidity stress tests — a change he says would have helped SVB avoid a disorderly failure in March 2023.

Nelson: SVB approached the Fed about signing up for the standing repo facility about a year before failing, to help pass internal liquidity stress tests, but the Fed said it 'wasn't ready to go there yet.'

Nelson: Silvergate Bank survived a ~60% deposit run in late 2022 by borrowing at the discount window against collateral, then self-liquidated in an orderly way with no FDIC cost — held up as how the lender-of-last-resort function should work.

Riksbank introduced a 0% interest deposit facility on a portion of bank reserves specifically to rebuild its capital without government recapitalization, motivated by central bank independence concerns.
e197109b-f5bc-473f-90df-6bf6d294167c.one_liner: Bill Nelson (BPI, ex-Fed) argues for shrinking the Fed's balance sheet, reforming liquidity rules to recognize discount-window/standing-repo access, and possibly reviving a demand-driven/ceiling reserve system — direct relevance to money-market plumbing but framed as forward-looking policy debate rather than immediate trade catalyst.
summary: Bill Nelson (BPI Chief Economist, ex-Fed) discusses a global 'sea change' toward smaller central bank balance sheets and demand-driven/ceiling reserve systems, citing ECB, BoE, Riksbank, Norges Bank, Bank of Canada and RBA all shrinking balance sheets partly to revive interbank markets.

He argues current liquidity requirements (LCR) wrongly ignore banks' capacity to borrow from the discount window/standing repo facility as a legitimate form of self-insurance, contributing to stigma and oversized reserve demand.

Discusses the new Fed balance-sheet task force under Chair Kevin Warsh, spurred by papers from Lorie Logan/Sam Schulhofer-Wolf, Stephen Miran, and Darrell Duffie; unclear whether the mandate covers just balance-sheet size or full operating-system redesign.
Recounts the Fed's historical below-market discount rate era (mid-1960s to 2003) and Volcker-era non-borrowed reserve targeting as a precedent for a demand-driven system with built-in borrowing.

Critiques Norway's tiered/quota reserve system as too heavy-handed versus a 'voluntary reserve target' approach (drawing on a 2008 Fed memo), though notes the voluntary version risks not reducing structural reserve demand enough unless priced correctly.

Cites central bank independence concerns (Riksbank's zero-interest reserve requirement to avoid government recapitalization, Bank of England's finance-ministry recapitalization, Quarles's 'attractive nuisance' quote) as another driver of the shrink-the-balance-sheet push.

Uses SVB (March 2023) and Silvergate (self-liquidation, late 2022) as case studies: SVB was denied standing repo facility access pre-failure and had to sell AFS securities, triggering a disorderly run; Silvergate successfully used the discount window to fund an orderly wind-down. Fed later (2024 FAQ) expanded standing repo/discount window/FHLB recognition for liquidity stress tests.

e1f6e282-2609-491c-b550-d1fc2626fc6b.recap: In this Fed Day interview, Danielle DiMartino Booth of QI Research reacts to a 25bp Fed hike under new chair Kevin Warsh, arguing the move and Warsh's press-conference tone amounted to unwarranted forward guidance despite his stated zero-forward-guidance policy. She notes the 2-year Treasury implies three more hikes priced in (one possibly before the election), the 10-year yield closed at 5.01%, its highest in 19 years, and stocks fell on the news. She disputes Warsh's claim that labor supply is keeping pace with job creation, citing data showing permanent job losers (27+ weeks unemployed) now exceed job switchers, which she calls a recessionary signal, and cites Bloomberg's Anna Wong on AI-driven displacement raising unemployment in exposed occupations. She discusses inflation internals: one-off increases in hotel CPI (Airbnb fee restructuring) and wireless pricing that should fade, alongside a BEA correction removing portfolio-management fees tied to rising equity markets from core PCE, offset by rising legal/bankruptcy-attorney fees flowing through PPI amid a surge in corporate bankruptcies (S&P counted 70+ filings with $2M+ liabilities for three straight months) and a rise in out-of-court distressed exchanges that often still end in bankruptcy court. She flags consumer stress (cash-out refinancers giving up low mortgage rates, tightening credit standards, falling real retail sales, trade-down from beef to chicken) concentrated below the top income tercile, which is itself now showing softening sentiment. Her biggest risk: AI capital investment has already peaked on an inflation-adjusted basis, propped up by accounting treatment of AI funding rounds flowing to hyperscaler earnings.

e75801e4-a708-11f1-b596-c7b325a74c17.recap: Alison Mass interviews Dipan Patel, co-managing partner and co-CEO of Permira, a roughly $100 billion private equity and credit firm. Patel recounts formative early jobs at Arthur Andersen during Enron and Lehman Brothers during the GFC, then describes Permira's model: mid-market private equity across consumer, healthcare, services and technology, split evenly between the US and Europe, with an 'artisanal' craftsman culture as a private partnership rather than a scaled 'factory' platform. He discusses AI's bifurcating effect on portfolio companies -- businesses with proprietary data, network effects and strong brands benefit, while commodity-data businesses decline -- and says Permira tracks how much of its NAV is exposed positively to AI model releases. He covers the industry-wide liquidity/DPI problem, noting the model needs roughly 20-25% distributions-to-paid-in per year versus an industry average near 10%, while Permira achieved 22% over the past year through disciplined exit processes and simply owning more desirable businesses. He describes Permira's culture as 'anti-fragile,' citing how the firm recovered from a distressed, over-levered, cyclical fund during the GFC by pivoting toward higher-quality, structurally growing businesses -- a strategy that still defines the firm today. He also discusses the firm's philanthropic foundation, now a permanent carry holder in its funds, his immigrant father's entrepreneurial background, and closes with a lightning-round on investing lessons and personal interests.
terms: DPI -- distributions to paid-in capital, cash returned to LPs as a percentage of invested/unrealized NAV

e7c52b24-a236-11f1-8bb8-cb2037ec9015.recap: Goldman Sachs' Alison Nathan and George Lee host GS Sustain's Brian Singer and utilities analyst Carly Davenport to update their AI power demand thesis. Davenport raised the US power demand CAGR to 3.5% through 2030, driven by data center demand hitting 108GW (up from 83GW) as new projects and rising data center utilization (vacancy down to 1-2%) both contribute. Singer noted hyperscaler capex estimates have jumped sharply since March (2027 estimate now $1.7tn, 2029 now $2.1tn), and despite efficiency gains, aggregate demand keeps outrunning them; globally, data center power demand in 2030 is now seen 170% above 2025 levels, equivalent to adding a country the size of Japan's total power consumption since 2024. They discuss regional market shifts (PJM staying dominant, MISO overtaking ERCOT as #2 by 2030), supply constraints via an expanded 'seven Ps' framework (pervasiveness, productivity, price, policy, parts, people, physical environment), and the rise of 'behind the meter' gas generation as a bridging solution (~30GW by 2030). Populist pushback and permitting delays (300+ local moratoria) are flagged as the steepest obstacle. On financing, Davenport notes regulated utility capex is up 60% over five years, funded ~30-50% with equity to preserve credit cushions, while independent power producers like Vistra and Constellation have seen investment-grade upgrades, with M&A-driven leverage expected to normalize toward 2x net debt/EBITDA within 12 months.

ecca2862-b38a-11f1-8ba3-5bdd634cc779.implications: For a repo/financing desk, the key read-throughs are: (1) natural real-money demand for 20-30yr paper is structurally shrinking as insurers rotate into floating-rate private credit, which argues for a steeper curve and higher term premium absent a risk-off catalyst; (2) Treasury's buyback/TGA mechanics are a liquidity-support and optics tool for off-the-runs, not a genuine debt-reduction or funding-supply relief valve, so don't expect it to ease bill/bond supply dynamics materially; (3) continued heavy IG corporate issuance for AI capex is a direct competitor for balance sheet against Treasuries, relevant to swap spreads and asset-swap levels.

Bush: Treasury buybacks reduce headline notional debt (buying discounted off-the-run bonds and reissuing at par) but do not materially reduce total interest cost

ecca2862-b38a-11f1-8ba3-5bdd634cc779.one_liner: A fixed-income CIO walks through why the long end is selling off, how insurance companies have quietly swapped natural long-Treasury demand for floating-rate private credit, and the mechanics (and limits) of Treasury's new buyback program.
ecca2862-b38a-11f1-8ba3-5bdd634cc779.recap: David Bush, CIO of Trajan Wealth and a former 18-year bond portfolio manager, discusses the six-month bond selloff (10-year up ~60bp, 30-year near 5.29% after crossing 5.3% in August). He attributes rising yields to $40 trillion in outstanding Treasury debt, tariff- and Iran-conflict-driven inflation, and heavy IG corporate issuance funding AI capex, which crowds out Treasury demand. The most detailed section covers the shifting buyer base for long-duration government paper: insurance companies, pensions and sovereign wealth funds are the natural buyers of 20-30 year bonds, but insurers have been reallocating a portion (roughly 7-15% of assets, per his due diligence) into private credit, which is largely floating-rate and thus near-zero duration, while keeping the rest of the book duration-matched to liabilities. He frames this as insurers dialing down duration and convexity risk while dialing up credit and liquidity risk to chase yield, and flags due-diligence concerns (loan tape access, delinquency data, interval-fund redemption gates capped near 5% of NAV per quarter). He then explains Treasury's buyback program in detail: increased from $2B to $4B (with $6B actually executed September 9), potentially funded via the TGA, aimed at supporting liquidity in illiquid off-the-run issues; he notes it can reduce headline notional debt (buying bonds back at a discount to par and reissuing at par) without materially changing total interest cost. The episode closes with views on gold/dollar dynamics, AI-driven equity sectors, and private credit skepticism generally.
terms: TGA -- Treasury General Account, the U.S. Treasury's operating cash account held at the Federal Reserve

f4d787ea-b117-11f1-9f76-630cadf4043c.recap: Goldman Sachs strategist George Cole discusses the broad, multi-decade-high rise in global government bond yields across the US, Germany, UK and Japan, arguing no single market or curve segment is driving it -- moves span the 30-year term-premium zone down to policy-rate-sensitive short maturities. Notably, the sell-off has occurred with low realized and implied volatility, which Cole argues signals a fundamentals-driven move rather than a technical dislocation. He attributes the rise to overlapping fundamentals: persistent large fiscal deficits since the pandemic, AI capex increasingly financed in debt markets competing with government borrowing for savings, resilient growth, and a recent energy-price spike (oil and European gas) linked to the war in Iran that has central banks (BoE, ECB, Fed) running low on patience with 'transitory' inflation shocks. He discusses the US Treasury's expanded long-end buyback program, arguing -- by analogy with the UK DMO's reduced 30-year issuance -- that such supply/liquidity operations affect relative curve shape and swap spreads but not the macro level of yields, which is set by fundamentals: inflation, fiscal trajectory and issuance competition. Cole frames current 5%+ 10-year US yields as a partial return to pre-GFC norms given a more symmetric, higher inflation distribution, but flags larger debt burdens as a key difference. Looking forward, he sees near-term downside risk to yields hinging on energy prices easing and medium-term downside risk from a slowdown or disinflationary surprise in the AI capex cycle, while fiscal tightening would also lower yields; he suggests duration may regain hedge value on a 2-4 year horizon.

f722623a-bd67-4af3-b5e4-db0ce09730cf.recap: The host argues the market and media are overreacting to the Treasury's announcement that it will double the pace of its coupon buyback operations, framing it as "QE lite" or stealth yield curve control. He contends this is misinformation from both critics (who want to cry money-printing) and the Treasury itself (which wants to change the subject away from the 30-year yield hitting its highest level since 2007 and total federal debt crossing $40 trillion). Mechanically, a buyback works by issuing slightly more T-bills than needed and using the extra cash to repurchase old "off-the-run" notes and bonds -- securities that trade thinly because liquidity concentrates in newly-issued "on-the-run" issues. He ties this directly to March 2020, when reserve managers dumping off-the-run Treasuries (driven by dollar shortage, not policy) overwhelmed dealer capacity to repo or resell them, which is the technical problem buybacks are meant to backstop. He traces buyback history from 1920s-30s programs through Clinton-era 2000 buybacks (when the government had a bond shortage), to Yellen's October 2022 talk and May 2024 launch (initially $2bn notes/bonds plus $500m TIPS), to today's doubling to roughly $4bn. He stresses the dollar amounts are trivial next to weekly bill auctions of $100bn+, and that gold's 3.6% pop the same day reflects a pre-existing rally since early August, not evidence of money printing.

Elson adds that stablecoin growth is fueling demand for tokenized yield products (money-market funds) and that crypto-native fintechs are now serious servicing competitors. Connexus reports $4 trillion transacted cumulatively and ~$7 billion/day currently, with atomic FX settlement across eight currencies including Hong Kong dollar and renminbi. Both speakers flag privacy/governance/finality on public chains and poor user experience/integration as the key remaining obstacles, predicting tokenization becomes invisible infrastructure within five years rather than a separate market.

marketmatters.podbean.com/427ea520-11aa-.recap: JPMorgan's Brian Long interviews Sam Teagle, CEO of ElectronX, a newly CFTC-registered power derivatives exchange (designated contract market and derivatives clearing organization) launched in ERCOT (Texas) in February and PJM in April. Teagle argues US power markets are at an inflection point: renewables are raising short-term intraday volatility on the supply side, while data centers and AI-driven load growth are surging on the demand side, yet power derivatives infrastructure remains underdeveloped relative to other asset classes. ElectronX's innovation is listing granular, centrally cleared hourly futures contracts (the next 120 hours at all times) on power hubs, allowing participants to trade and settle exposure to specific hour-endings rather than broad daily/monthly blocks. Trades clear anonymously through the exchange (no bilateral ISDAs), settle against real-time price prints, and credit/debit accounts within seconds. The exchange trades 7am-8pm Chicago time on weekdays (not yet 24/7 or weekends, though that's on the roadmap), has direct market access with lowered barriers to entry, and has attracted over 50 institutional participants including retail energy providers, bitcoin miners, data centers, utilities, and quant trading firms, though daily volume remains modest (~1,000 contracts/day). Teagle frames this as building financial infrastructure to help the grid transition attract private capital by giving participants tools to hedge short-term price risk more precisely.

marketmatters.podbean.com/93ac6a2f-aaa3-.recap: In this JPMorgan Making Sense episode, Meridith Cleary speaks with Carlos Gomez Gascon, JPMorgan's head of EM rates e-trading, about how automation is changing EM rates markets. Gascon distinguishes electronification (sending price requests via electronic channels, but still manually priced) from automation (machine-generated pricing and hedging), arguing EM lags developed markets partly due to local regulation, episodic liquidity, and varying broker/futures market infrastructure. He frames EM rates as an ecosystem of three linked asset classes -- FX swaps (priced off SOFR curve, local IRS curve, and cross-currency basis), interest rate swaps, and bonds (linked to swaps via a stable bond basis) -- so improving automation in one improves pricing across all three. IRS leads electronification because of lower capital costs and better tenor standardization, making it attractive to hedge funds for backtesting. Local bond markets are automating too, driven by asset managers trading in baskets that are hard to price manually. A key regional distinction: EMEA and Latam repo markets function well, keeping buy/sell bond prices aligned, while APAC repo markets are often hard to access, meaning dealers without inventory struggle to borrow bonds to deliver, creating pricing distortions between buy and sell sides. Brazil and Korea benefit from liquid interest rate futures aiding hedging and price discovery. Systematic funds are a growing EM client base, benefiting from faster, data-driven price discovery. During volatility, dealers lean more on automated skew/spread quoting rather than manual per-deal pricing. Benchmark reforms (e.g., South Africa's move to ZARONIA) typically follow a manual-to-electronic-to-automated adoption path.

omfif.podbean.com/36f449e9-f04f-3326-bc3.recap: Former Norges Bank governor Øystein Olsen discusses a new book, Our Rich Country, written with historian Eivind Tomasson, rebutting Martin Bech Holte's bestselling The Country That Became Too Rich. Holte argues Norway enjoyed a 'golden age' of growth until roughly 2013-14, after which oil wealth bred complacency, weak productivity, and a bloated public sector, prescribing sharp cuts to government spending. Olsen counters that Holte cherry-picks data and mislabels a run of external shocks -- the financial crisis, the 2014 oil price collapse, the pandemic, and the war in Ukraine -- as internally caused laziness. Olsen defends Norway's fiscal rule, which limits spending of oil revenue to the fund's expected real return, preserving wealth for future generations, and argues having a large sovereign asset is preferable to the high government debt burdening many peer economies. He draws a parallel between Holte's rhetoric and the MAGA-style narrative that institutions and politicians are corrupt, warning this undermines public confidence. The conversation touches on Norway's generous aid to Ukraine, a possible role for NBIM in Arctic/defense-adjacent infrastructure (echoing Mark Carney's push for Nordic pension capital), and NBIM chief Nicolai Tangen's warning that a severe market correction could theoretically wipe out the fund, which Olsen sees as a needed reminder to reduce fiscal dependency on fund transfers rather than a signal of complacency, though he calls the scenario itself unrealistic since fiscal policy would adjust before that point.
terms: NBIM -- Norges Bank Investment Management, manager of Norway's sovereign wealth (oil) fund

omfif.podbean.com/c14167df-0da2-3e71-bef.recap: This episode of UMFIF's Invested podcast features Tram Anh Nguyen, co-founder of the Center for Finance, Technology and Entrepreneurship (CFTE) and chairwoman of Global Women in AI, discussing the underrepresentation of women in artificial intelligence roles and leadership. Nguyen argues that inclusivity in AI is an economic and resilience issue, not just a diversity one, since systems reflect the judgment of those who design and govern them. She discusses CFTE's white paper 'AIfication of Talents,' which argues competitive advantage will come from 'talent density' -- how many people can contribute effectively in an AI-augmented environment -- and that retention should be treated as a board-level structural issue rather than an HR problem. She uses the 2014 Amazon recruiting-AI example (biased against CVs mentioning 'women') to illustrate algorithmic bias, proposing a three-level fix: model-level data testing and monitoring, human-level cognitive diversity and AI literacy, and institutional-level governance frameworks with clear accountability for who builds, validates, and can override algorithms. She references UNESCO's ethics-of-AI recommendations and CFTE's own AI Proficiency Framework (literacy, applied practitioner, systems/decision leader levels). The conversation closes on optimism about Global Women in AI's cross-sector community spanning industry, policy, and regulation across London, Riyadh, Abu Dhabi, Singapore, and Hong Kong.
